summary:
LunarSight is an interactive 3D landing site explorer and mission-window planner built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Lunar south-polar missions face severe terrain shadowing and erratic Earth visibility due to low solar elevation (< 2°) and rugged topography.

LunarSight eliminates the complexity of traditional GIS tools by uniting a Three.js curved-terrain viewer (rendered off-main-thread via Web Workers) with a synchronized 360° panoramic horizon mask and a 1×–60× UTC timeline. Using NASA PGDA LOLA elevation models (5 m to 480 m) and JPL Horizons ephemerides across 15 Artemis candidate sites, it delivers instant calculations of cumulative sunlight, longest continuous darkness periods, and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight.

By enabling rapid side-by-side A/B site comparison, LunarSight empowers mission planners to quickly adapt to schedule slips while making polar lunar science accessible to students and the public.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

LunarSight is an interactive 3D lunar south-polar landing site explorer and mission-window planner built to resolve the complex lighting and communication challenges of polar lunar exploration. Missions to the lunar South Pole face extreme conditions: the Sun hovers near the horizon at grazing angles (< 2°), and crater rims cast long, dynamic shadows that can plunge landing sites into weeks of darkness or sever line-of-sight communications with Earth.

LunarSight unites these critical factors into an intuitive, high-performance web cockpit:

  • Curved 3D Local Terrain Viewer: Built with Three.js (v0.187.0) and executed off the main thread via Web Workers, the viewer dynamically constructs welded, multi-resolution terrain meshes directly onto the true 1,737,400 m lunar sphere across five radial density bands (from 100 m high-detail zones up to 150 km far-field horizons).
  • Synchronized 360° Panoramic Horizon Mask: Ray-marches local topography to construct a complete azimuthal skyline obstruction profile. Topocentric trajectories of the Sun and Earth are plotted directly against this skyline, instantly revealing geometric eclipses and line-of-sight blockages.
  • Interactive UTC Simulation & Timeline: Users can scrub or animate time from 1× to 60× speeds across custom mission intervals. The engine computes time-weighted sunlight duration, longest continuous darkness runs, and direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility with automated next-event countdowns (sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, Earthset).
  • Side-by-Side A/B Site Comparison: Planners can directly contrast two candidate sites (e.g., Artemis Site 01 Connecting Ridge vs. Site 04 Shackleton Rim) under identical epochs, cadences, and observer mast heights.

What benefits does it have?

  • Unified Mission Cockpit: Eliminates the fragmented workflow of consulting separate GIS desktop software, raw ASCII ephemeris tables, and static 2D shadow maps. All critical spatial and temporal variables are synchronized in real time.
  • Direct Operational Answers: Delivers immediate, decision-critical mission metrics—most notably the longest uninterrupted darkness period (vital for sizing battery reserves and thermal survival) and Earth communication blackout windows.
  • Zero-Install, Cross-Platform Accessibility: Runs natively in any modern web browser via WebGL without plugins, specialized hardware, or proprietary licenses.
  • Fluid, Non-Blocking Performance: Offloading geometry generation, decimation, and ray-sampling to background Web Workers guarantees a responsive 60 FPS interface without UI freezing during intensive computations.
  • Scientific Transparency: Implements explicit provenance metadata badges distinguishing source-derived data, synthetic benchmarks, and explicit observer parameters, upholding strict scientific integrity.

What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Accelerating Mission Trade-Off Studies: As Artemis, CLPS commercial landers, and international missions face tight launch windows and schedule slips, planners can rapidly evaluate alternative landing sites, dates, and antenna/solar mast heights in minutes rather than days.
  • Democratizing Lunar Science Education: Complex celestial mechanics—such as lunar libration, topocentric parallax, and extreme polar shadow dynamics—become visually intuitive and interactive for university students, educators, and the public.
  • Informing Lunar Resource Architecture: Enables teams to assess trade-offs between illuminated ridgelines (ideal for solar power generation and Earth radio links) and nearby cold traps in Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) containing volatile water-ice resources.

Tools, Technologies & Data Sources

  • Frontend & 3D Graphics: TypeScript (strict mode), React 18, Vite, Three.js (v0.187.0) for 3D curved surface rendering and celestial directional lighting; Lucide icons and Geist typography.
  • Concurrency & Web Workers: Native HTML5 Web Workers for off-main-thread terrain triangulation, radial LOD mesh generation, and horizon mask calculation.
    • NASA Planetary Geodynamics Data Archive (PGDA): Product 78 (LOLA 5 m/px Artemis candidate sites DEMs) and Product 90 (LOLA South Polar DEM mosaics at 40 m and 480 m resolution).
    • NASA JPL Horizons System API: High-precision topocentric Sun and Earth ephemeris vectors accounting for lunar libration and finite-distance Earth parallax.
    • NASA Moon Trek & LROC QuickMap (Arizona State University): Surface landmark reference and coordinate cross-verification.
  • Quality Assurance & Deployment: Vitest (100+ automated unit and integration tests covering coordinate transformations, horizon raymarching, and scenario state machines) and Vercel cloud hosting.

Key Innovations & Creative Highlights

  • Dual-Perspective Geometric Synergy: LunarSight simultaneously bridges an exocentric 3D orbital view of the terrain with an egocentric 360° panoramic horizon skyline. Planners do not just see numbers—they visually perceive why Earth dips below a crater rim or when the Sun emerges through a mountain notch.
  • Concentric Radial Mesh Architecture: Instead of planar projections that distort polar geometry, LunarSight models terrain natively on the lunar sphere with radial multi-resolution rings (dense 5 m resolution near the lander, progressively transitioning outward to 150 km) with crack-free ring welding.
  • Tactical Event Countdown: Rather than just static status displays, the timeline actively scans forward to detect and snap to impending operational transitions (e.g., "Next Sunset in 14h 20m"), acting like a real-time flight director’s countdown clock.
  • Built-in Provenance & Uncertainty Integrity: Uniquely exposes the origin and limits of every dataset (distinguishing real LOLA data from mock baseline models and explicitly reporting nulls instead of assuming zero terrain).

Technical & Operational Considerations

  • Extreme Polar Lighting Physics: Accounting for solar grazing angles (< 2°), lack of atmospheric scattering, sharp high-contrast shadowing, and the critical distinction between geometric sun visibility and actual photovoltaic power generation.
  • Observer & Mast Height Sensitivity: Modeling equipment elevation above ground (from 1 m rover masts to 10 m habitat towers), as a few meters of elevation on a polar ridge can make the difference between weeks of continuous power and devastating darkness.
  • Far-Field Terrain Obstructions: Acknowledging that peaks located 50–100 km away frequently cast shadows at the lunar South Pole, requiring a generous 150 km calculation radius rather than relying solely on local elevation patches.
  • Lunar Libration & Earth Parallax: Implementing true topocentric coordinates from JPL Horizons to capture the Moon's orbital wobble, which causes Earth to trace apparent loops across the polar horizon.
  • Data Volume vs. Web Performance: Managing multi-gigabyte LOLA elevation rasters through intelligent offline radial sampling and client-side LRU caching, delivering sub-second interactive loads on standard consumer web browsers.
